propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of a Senior Immigration Officer's May 4, 2020 decision refusing permanent residence on H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision by a Senior Immigration Officer [Officer], dated May 4, 2020, refusing the Applicant’s application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds [Decision].

propositions.text: The Officer found Applicants lacked sufficient H&C considerations to grant exemption under section 25(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Officer found the Applicants did not have sufficient H&C considerations to grant an exemption under section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of a May 4, 2020 Officer decision refusing permanent residence on H&C grounds; the Officer found insufficient H&C considerations.

propositions.text: Applicants are Ethiopian citizens; Principal Applicant is Mulugeta, spouse Elizabeth, with a 24-year-old daughter and 17-year-old son.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of Ethiopia. The Principal Applicant is Mulugeta and Elizabeth is his spouse. They have a daughter (age 24), and a son (age 17) [Minor Applicant].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants are Ethiopian citizens: Principal Applicant Mulugeta, spouse Elizabeth, with a 24-year-old daughter and 17-year-old son.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant is a Nuclear Safeguards Inspector for IAEA, based in Vienna, reporting to UN Security Council and General Assembly.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant is a Nuclear Safeguards Inspector employed by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), an international body based in Vienna which reports to the United Nations Security Council and the United Nations General Assembly.

propositions.text: Before Canada assignment, Applicants lived in Vienna due to Principal Applicant's IAEA work.
propositions.quote: Before being assigned to work in Canada, the Applicants lived in Vienna based on the Principal Applicant’s work as an official for the IAEA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Principal Applicant works for IAEA in Vienna and the Applicants lived there before Canada assignment.

propositions.text: Applicants came to Canada in 2013 for Principal Applicant's 5-year IAEA posting in Toronto, with Temporary Resident Visas renewed to extend stay.
propositions.quote: In 2013, the Applicants came to Canada based on the Principal Applicant’s 5-year posting to the IAEA’s regional office in Toronto. The Applicants were issued Temporary Resident Visas which they renewed to extend their stay.

propositions.text: Though intending temporary stay in 2013, Applicants applied for permanent residence on H&C grounds in 2017.
propositions.quote: Although their intention in 2013 was to stay in Canada temporarily, they applied for permanent residence on H&C grounds in 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicants came to Canada in 2013 for a 5-year posting, initially temporary, but applied for permanent residence in 2017.

propositions.text: Officer was not satisfied Applicants' H&C situation was exceptional to justify exemption under section 25(1) IRPA and dismissed application on May 4, 2020.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not satisfied the Applicants’ H&C situation was exceptional so as to justify an exemption under section 25(1) of the IRPA and dismissed their application on May 4, 2020.

propositions.text: H&C grounds raised were establishment, best interests of the child, and hardship upon return.
propositions.quote: The H&C grounds raised were establishment, best interests of the child, and hardship upon return.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Applicants' H&C situation not exceptional and dismissed application; grounds were establishment, child's best interests, and hardship.

propositions.text: Officer gave positive consideration to Applicants' stable employment, church attendance, volunteerism, and community involvement.
propositions.quote: the Officer gave some positive consideration to the Applicants’ demonstrated history of stable employment in Canada, albeit as an international agency employee who was obliged to return to Vienna upon the conclusion of his assignment, their history of church attendance and volunteerism, and their community involvement.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged steps towards establishment but found no exceptional degree of establishment in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Officer acknowledged steps the Applicants have taken towards establishing themselves but ultimately found they had not achieved an exceptional degree of establishment during their time in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker acknowledged Applicants' stable employment and community involvement but found no exceptional establishment in Canada.

propositions.text: Officer noted family will return to Austria; Principal Applicant must return to maintain employment.
propositions.quote: the Officer noted the Principal Applicant, his wife, and son have indicated they will be returning to Austria, and that the Principal Applicant is required to return to Austria to maintain his employment.

propositions.text: Applicants are well established in Austria with good income and rental property ensuring successful reintegration.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are well established in Austria where he will be well paid (as is the case in Canada) and where he also owns a rental property generating an additional $4,000.00 a month income, thereby ensuring their successful reintegration on relocation from Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker noted family plans to return to Austria where they are well established with income and property.

propositions.text: Daughter may not follow family to Austria due to age limit for diplomats' children but may have other EU options, no evidence of efforts provided.
propositions.quote: the Officer acknowledged the daughter might be unable to follow the rest of the family to Austria because children of diplomats are unable to follow their parents past the age of 21. However, the Officer noted she may have other avenues available to remain in the European Union [EU] but had not provided evidence of making an effort in that regard.

propositions.text: Officer assessed daughter's hardship if returned to Ethiopia, noting adjustment period but strong family ties and support for re-establishment.
propositions.quote: The Officer assessed her hardship if returned to Ethiopia. The Officer reviewed the situation for women, the economy, and healthcare in Ethiopia, along with impact of family separation. The Officer found she will likely experience a period of adjustment; however, with her strong ties in Ethiopia and support from her parents and family, she would be able to re-establish herself in her country of nationality.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found daughter may not follow family to Austria but could remain in EU; if returned to Ethiopia, she would adjust and re-establish with family support.

propositions.text: Officer accepted return to Ethiopia would challenge Minor Applicant but family plans to return to Austria where he would remain in parents' care.
propositions.quote: the Officer accepted a return to Ethiopia would pose challenges for the Minor Applicant. However, the Officer acknowledged the family is not looking to return to Ethiopia and the evidence demonstrated the Minor Applicant would be remaining in the care of his parents, and thus returning to Austria.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker accepted challenges for Minor Applicant if returned to Ethiopia but noted family plans to return to Austria where he would remain with parents.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged Minor Applicant's bullying but found it a worldwide issue and insufficient evidence it was ethnic-based.
propositions.quote: the Officer acknowledged he may have experienced some bullying in school, but found bullying of adolescents within educational institutions to be a worldwide issue. Moreover, the Officer found the evidence was insufficient to suggest the bullying he experienced was due to his ethnicity.

propositions.text: Officer concluded it is in Minor Applicant's best interests to follow parents to Austria and remain in their care while applying for permanent residence normally.
propositions.quote: The Officer concluded it would be in the best interests of the Minor Applicant to follow his parents to Austria to remain in the care of his primary caregivers while the family applies for permanent residence in the normal fashion.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Minor Applicant's bullying not ethnic-based and concluded best interests are to follow parents to Austria and remain in their care.

propositions.text: Issues: Did Officer err in assessing establishment, hardship upon return, and best interests of the child?
propositions.quote: The issues raised are as follows: Did the Officer err in their assessment of the Applicants’ establishment? Did the Officer err in their assessment of hardship upon return? Did the Officer err in their assessment of best interests of the child?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: whether the Officer erred in assessing establishment, hardship upon return, and best interests of the child.

propositions.text: Canada Post explains a reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law; reviewing court must examine reasons with respectful attention.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is “one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov, at para. 85). Accordingly, when conducting reasonableness review “[a] reviewing court must begin its inquiry into the reasonableness of a decision by examining the reasons provided with ‘respectful attention’ and seeking to understand the reasoning process followed by the decision maker to arrive at [the] conclusion” (Vavilov, at para. 84, quoting Dunsmuir, at para. 48).

propositions.text: Reasons should be read holistically and contextually to understand basis of decision; court considers if decision bears hallmarks of reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The reasons should be read holistically and contextually in order to understand “the basis on which a decision was made” (Vavilov, at para. 97, citing Newfoundland Nurses). [32] A reviewing court should consider whether the decision as a whole is reasonable: “what is reasonable in a given situation will always depend on the constraints imposed by the legal and factual context of the particular decision under review” (Vavilov, at para. 90). The reviewing court must ask “whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility – and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision” (Vavilov, at para. 99, citing Dunsmuir, at paras 47 and 74, and Catalyst Paper Corp. v. North Cowichan (District), 2012 SCC 2, [2012] 1 S.C.R. 5, at para. 13).

propositions.text: Under reasonableness review, burden is on challenger to show decision is unreasonable due to central or significant flaws.
propositions.quote: Under reasonableness review, “[t]he burden is on the party challenging the decision to show that it is unreasonable” (Vavilov, at para. 100). The challenging party must satisfy the court “that any shortcomings or flaws relied on ... are sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable” (Vavilov, at para. 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Canada Post and Vavilov: reasonableness requires coherent, justified reasons; burden is on challenger to show unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Decision's internal rationality questioned if reasons show logical fallacies; court must be satisfied reasoning 'adds up'.
propositions.quote: the internal rationality of a decision may be called into question if the reasons exhibit clear logical fallacies, such as circular reasoning, false dilemmas, unfounded generalizations or an absurd premise. ... a reviewing court must ultimately be satisfied that the decision maker’s reasoning “adds up”.

propositions.text: Decision must be justified in relation to relevant law and facts; legal and factual contexts constrain decision-maker.
propositions.quote: a decision, to be reasonable, must be justified in relation to the constellation of law and facts that are relevant to the decision: Dunsmuir, at para. 47; Catalyst, at para. 13; Nor-Man Regional Health Authority, at para. 6. Elements of the legal and factual contexts of a decision operate as constraints on the decision maker in the exercise of its delegated powers.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Vavilov: decision must be free of logical fallacies and justified by relevant law and facts.

propositions.text: Vavilov requires reasons to justify decision to those affected; decision must be reasonable in light of evidentiary record and factual matrix.
propositions.quote: “it is not enough for the outcome of a decision to be justifiable. Where reasons for a decision are required, the decision must also be justified, by way of those reasons, by the decision-maker to those to whom the decision applies,” and provides guidance that the reviewing court review decide based on the record before them: ... The reasonableness of a decision may be jeopardized where the decision maker has fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Vavilov: reasons must justify decision to affected parties and be reasonable based on evidence and facts before decision-maker.

propositions.text: Vavilov states reviewing court must not reweigh evidence absent exceptional circumstances; decision-maker's factual findings are deferred to.
propositions.quote: It is trite law that the decision maker may assess and evaluate the evidence before it and that, absent exceptional circumstances, a reviewing court will not interfere with its factual findings. The reviewing court must refrain from “reweighing and reassessing the evidence considered by the decision maker”

propositions.text: Reasons for deference include judicial efficiency, certainty, public confidence, and decision-maker's advantageous position.
propositions.quote: many of the same reasons that support an appellate court’s deferring to a lower court’s factual findings, including the need for judicial efficiency, the importance of preserving certainty and public confidence, and the relatively advantageous position of the first instance decision maker, apply equally in the context of judicial review

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Vavilov: reviewing court must defer to decision-maker's factual findings absent exceptional circumstances.

propositions.text: Applicants request extension of time for judicial review application due to missed statutory deadlines.
propositions.quote: The Applicants made submissions requesting an extension of time, because they did not meet usual statutory timelines for filing an application for leave and judicial review.

propositions.text: Respondent submits no extension needed as deadline fell within COVID-19 suspension period for federal statutory time limits.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits, and I agree, there is no need to grant an extension of time because “the Applicants’ deadline to apply for leave and judicial review fell within the suspension period running from March 13, 2020 and September 13, 2020” which is applicable to “statutory time periods in federal legislation for starting proceedings” in the Federal Court.

propositions.text: Court agrees no extension of time is needed due to COVID-19 suspension period.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits, and I agree, there is no need to grant an extension of time because “the Applicants’ deadline to apply for leave and judicial review fell within the suspension period running from March 13, 2020 and September 13, 2020” which is applicable to “statutory time periods in federal legislation for starting proceedings” in the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants request extension of time; Respondent and court agree no extension needed due to COVID-19 suspension period.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer erred in assessing establishment despite significant evidence provided.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred in assessing their establishment because they say they provided significant evidence in support of their establishment.

propositions.text: Applicants rely on IP5 Guide and prior cases confirming factors for assessing establishment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the IP5 Guide for H&C applications list factors for measuring establishment, noting this Court has confirmed and adopted these factor for assessing establishment, see Hee Lee v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 368 [Shore J] at para 18 and Ahmad v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 646 [Dawson J] at para 44-45.

propositions.text: Court finds Applicants failed to persuade based on record; no need to repeat evidence in reasons.
propositions.quote: With respect, and in my view, the Applicants failed to persuade me based on the record in this case which need not be repeated in these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer erred assessing establishment; court finds Applicants failed to persuade based on record.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer erred by requiring evidence of 'exceptional' establishment without explaining 'exceptional'.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred by requiring the Applicants provide evidence of an exceptional degree of establishment yet failed to explain what constitutes “exceptional”.

propositions.text: Applicants rely on Apura to argue absence of exceptional circumstances is incorrect legal standard for denial.
propositions.quote: The Applicants rely on Apura v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 762 [Ahmed J] at para 23 to argue when the absence of exceptional circumstances forms the basis of a decision maker’s analysis denying relief, this imposes an incorrect legal standard.

propositions.text: Preponderance of jurisprudence, including Huang and Li, holds contrary to Applicants' argument on 'exceptional' standard.
propositions.quote: However, the preponderance of jurisprudence (including my decision in Li v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 187 at paras 25-26) is outlined in Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 265 [Huang] at para 21 [Crampton CJ] at para 21 and is to the contrary.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer erred requiring 'exceptional' establishment without explanation; court finds jurisprudence holds contrary.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Officer erred discounting Principal Applicant's employment as not tied to Canada and ignoring willingness to seek Canadian employment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred in discounting the Principal Applicant’s employment because it was not tied to Canada – indeed he had to leave to keep his job - while ignoring his willingness to acquire comparable employment in Canada.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant stated in affidavit he considered Canadian employment and had informal discussions with potential employers.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant stated in his affidavit he has considered gaining employment with a Canadian-based employer and informal discussions have taken place with potential employers.

propositions.text: Court views this as weighing evidence, a matter for decision-maker, not for reviewing court per Vavilov para 125.
propositions.quote: In my view, this is simply a matter of weighing and assessing evidence, a matter withheld from reviewing judges per para 125 in Vavilov quoted above.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer erred discounting employment and ignoring job search; court says weighing evidence is decision-maker's role.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably considered establishment linked to diplomatic posting and expected relocation.
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably considered establishment, which flowed from the Principal Applicant’s diplomatic work assignment and found relocation was expected of individuals who work for international organizations.

propositions.text: Applicants' ties to Canada not exceptional compared to others in similar situations per Puri and Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: I agree the Applicants’ “ties to Canada did not depend on circumstances beyond their control and were in no way exceptional or atypical as compared with other people in their situation”, see Puri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 132 [Martineau J] at para 19, citing to Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 [Abella J] at para 26.

propositions.text: No unreasonableness in Officer's finding on establishment; it was open on the record.
propositions.quote: There is no unreasonableness in this finding which was open on this record.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer reasonably considered establishment linked to diplomatic posting; ties not exceptional; no unreasonableness found.

propositions.text: Officer erred in finding Applicants' departure will not impact their community, contrary to evidence including a 2015 Bikila award
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred in finding the Applicants’ departure will not impact their community as this was contrary to the evidence. The Applicants submit the Officer failed to consider evidence such as the Principal Applicant receiving a Bikila award in 2015

propositions.text: Officer reasonably assessed relevant factors and was not obliged to cite every piece of evidence submitted
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably assessed the relevant factors noting H&C officers are under no obligation to cite every piece of evidence submitted

propositions.text: Officer could not conclude Applicants' case was exceptional, which was the Officer's role
propositions.quote: At the end of the day, the Officer was not able to conclude the Applicants’ case was exceptional. That was the Officer’s job

propositions.text: Court's role on judicial review is not to re-litigate the record before the Officer
propositions.quote: while it seems the Court is being asked to re-litigate the record before the Officer, that is not the job of this Court on judicial review

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer erred on community impact and evidence; Court finds Officer reasonably assessed factors and judicial review cannot re-litigate facts.

propositions.text: Applicants provided corroborating evidence of hardship if applying for permanent residence outside Canada
propositions.quote: The Applicants say they provided corroborating evidence of the hardship they face if required to apply for permanent residence from outside Canada

propositions.text: Officer reasonably considered conditions in Austria where Applicants will return, noting education, home ownership, and employment
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably considered conditions in Austria, as the Principal Applicant, his wife, and the Minor Applicant will be returning to Austria, not Ethiopia. The Officer found the Applicants would be able to re-establish themselves in Austria in light of their high levels of education, home ownership, and the Principal Applicant’s existing employment with the IAEA

propositions.text: Court agrees Officer's finding is reasonable given facts and law
propositions.quote: I am unable to agree this finding is anything but reasonable given the facts and constraining law

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say they showed hardship evidence; Court finds Officer reasonably considered Austria conditions and finds decision reasonable.

propositions.text: Daughter might be unable to follow family to Austria but Officer found little evidence she tried and failed to secure status there
propositions.quote: While the daughter might possibly be unable to follow her family to Austria, the Officer reasonably found little to no evidence to demonstrate she attempted and was unable to secure status in Austria since turning 21 two years ago

propositions.text: Officer found other avenues available to daughter to remain in EU if family resides there
propositions.quote: The Officer found this did not preclude “other avenues available to her to remain in EU, if her entire nuclear family resides there.”

propositions.text: Onus is on Applicants to establish grounds for exceptional relief in H&C review
propositions.quote: the onus is and remained on the Applicants to establish grounds for the exceptional relief conveyed by a positive H&C review: see Goraya v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 341 [Fothergill J] at para 16

propositions.text: Applicants failed on factual matter made by Officer; Court not persuaded to intervene per Vavilov para 125
propositions.quote: In this connection they failed on a factual matter made by the Officer; I am not persuaded to intervene, per Vavilov at para 125

paragraphs.summary: Court finds daughter lacked evidence to show inability to secure status in Austria; onus on Applicants; no intervention warranted.

propositions.text: Officer erred in finding daughter familiar with Ethiopian culture despite living mostly outside Ethiopia
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred in finding the daughter was familiar with Ethiopian culture despite having lived most of her life outside Ethiopia

propositions.text: Daughter will face hardship more than ordinary for someone leaving a country where they spent some time, citing Irimie
propositions.quote: the daughter will face hardship that is more than “what would ordinarily be expected of someone leaving a country where they have spent some time”, see Irimie v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2000] FCJ No 1906 [Pelletier J] at para 12

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer erred on daughter's cultural familiarity and hardship exceeding ordinary expectations.

propositions.text: Officer was contradictory in finding daughter could re-establish only with parents' financial support
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that in finding the daughter will be able to re-establish herself as a highly educated woman, but only with the help of her parents’ financial support, the Officer was contradictory

propositions.text: Officer did not find that; was entitled to weigh education and parental support against adverse country conditions
propositions.quote: I note this is not what the Officer found. Moreover, the Officer was entitled to weigh her education and ability to draw support from her parents against adverse country conditions regarding women with low education; see Caleb v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 1018 [McHaffie J] at para 28

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say Officer was contradictory on daughter's re-establishment; Court finds Officer did not so find and was entitled to weigh factors.

propositions.text: Officer erred in assessing human rights in Ethiopia and ignored relevant evidence in National Documentation Package (NDP)
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer erred in assessing the human rights conditions in Ethiopia and ignored relevant evidence contained in the National Documentation Package [NDP]

propositions.text: NDP is not extrinsic evidence and should have been considered, citing political changes and prison system
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the NDP is not extrinsic to the Record and should have been considered by the Officer, pointing to extracts from the NDP regarding political changes brought by Prime Minister Abiy’s regime and Ethiopia’s prison system

propositions.text: NDP is extrinsic evidence in H&C context, per Hoyte 2015 FC 175 para 14
propositions.quote: the NDP is extrinsic evidence in the context of an H&C application, as found by Justice Strickland in Hoyte v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 175 at para 14

propositions.text: Onus is on Applicants to put forward factors for Officer's consideration, per Santiago 2020 FC 198 para 59
propositions.quote: the onus was upon the Applicants to put forward the factors that they wanted the Officer to consider”; see Santiago v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 198 [Russell J] at para 59

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer ignored NDP evidence which is not extrinsic; Court finds NDP is extrinsic and onus on Applicants to present factors.

propositions.text: Officer failed to analyze daughter's hardship considering establishment, life outside Ethiopia, and adverse conditions; erred by not applying totality of evidence
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Officer did not analyze the daughter’s hardship considering her establishment, her life spent mostly outside Ethiopia, and adverse country conditions, all of which constitute a sufficient degree of hardship. The Applicants submit the Officer erred in deciding the case at bar without applying the totality of the evidence to the daughter’s situation

propositions.text: Cites Liyanage 2005 FC 1045 to support argument
propositions.quote: citing to Liyanage v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 1045 [Lufty CJ as he was then]

propositions.text: Liyanage rejected submission that officer did not consider evidence in totality
propositions.quote: this was not the dicta in Liyanage and instead, Chief Justice Lufty rejected the applicant’s submission that “the officer did not consider the evidence placed before her in its totality”

propositions.text: Request to re-litigate case is outside judicial review parameters per Vavilov
propositions.quote: this seems to be a request to re-litigate the case which Vavilov notes, is outside the parameters of judicial review

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer failed to analyze daughter's hardship fully; Court finds Liyanage rejects this and re-litigation is outside judicial review.

propositions.text: Minor Applicant will face hardship if returned to Ethiopia; Officer erred on bullying evidence and made veiled credibility finding without hearing
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit the Minor Applicant will face hardship if returned to Ethiopia; however, it has been established the Minor Applicant will return to Austria with his parents and not Ethiopia. The Applicants also submit the Minor Applicant suffered from bullying in Austria because of his ethnicity and the Officer erred by stating the bullying could have occurred for other reasons. The Applicants submit the Officer’s doubts regarding the bullying of the Minor Applicant amounted to a veiled credibility finding and a hearing should have been conferred

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Minor Applicant faces hardship and Officer erred on bullying evidence and credibility without hearing.

propositions.text: Officer did not make veiled credibility findings but noted lack of particulars on bullying from authorities or family
propositions.quote: The Officer did not make veiled credibility findings. Rather, the Officer’s concern was the Applicant had neglected to provide any particulars on bullying from school authorities, the minor Applicant’s parents, or the minor Applicant himself

propositions.text: Cites Zhang 2020 FC 503 paras 18-19 on evidence requirements
propositions.quote: see Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 503 [McDonald J] at paras 18-19

propositions.text: There was insufficient evidence on bullying from Applicants
propositions.quote: There simply was not enough evidence put forward by the Applicants on this point

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer did not make veiled credibility findings but noted insufficient bullying evidence from Applicants.

propositions.text: Applicants have not shown Officer's decision was unreasonable
propositions.quote: the Applicants have not shown the decision of the Officer was unreasonable

propositions.text: Applicants did not show exceptional establishment for diplomat's family or hardship returning to country of employment and assets
propositions.quote: These Applicants did not demonstrate how their establishment was exceptional for the family of a diplomat; they did not demonstrate how they would face hardship in returning to a country where they will be gainfully employed, housed, have substantial assets and lived for many years

propositions.text: Daughter did not show efforts to obtain status in Austria or EU
propositions.quote: the daughter did not demonstrate any efforts to show she would be unable to obtain status in Austria or the EU

propositions.text: Officer reasonably assessed Minor Applicant's best interests
propositions.quote: the Officer reasonably assessed the best interests of the Minor Applicant

propositions.text: Decision is transparent, intelligible and justified on facts and law
propositions.quote: In my view, the Decision is transparent, intelligible and justified based on the facts and law

propositions.text: Judicial review is dismissed
propositions.quote: Therefore, judicial review will be dismissed

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Officer's decision was reasonable and dismisses judicial review.

propositions.text: No question of general importance proposed or arising
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a question of general importance, and none arises

propositions.text: Judgment: judicial review dismissed, no question certified, no costs order
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that judicial review is dismissed, no question is certified and there is no order as to costs

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review, no question certified, no costs ordered.
